titre: The piece of door that brought down an accusation
accroche: Argentina, 1892. A neighbor is tortured to make him confess to a double murder. An inspector would rather saw off a piece of door.
contenu_vulgarise:
Necochea, Buenos Aires province, June 29, 1892. Two children are found dead in their home: Ponciano, six, and Feliza, four. Their mother, Francisca Rojas, twenty-seven, has a wound to her throat and accuses a neighbor, Pedro Ramón Velázquez. The local police do what police did then: they question the man relentlessly, and according to several accounts of the case they lock him up for a night with the children's bodies to break him. He denies everything, without pause.

## Evidence that depends on no one

An inspector from the central police, Álvarez, is sent from La Plata as reinforcement. On a door he notices a print left in blood. Rather than describe it in a report, he saws out the panel and takes the piece of wood back to La Plata, where he compares the print with those of the people present. It is the mother's.

Álvarez had been trained by Juan Vucetich, an immigrant from Dalmatia employed by the Buenos Aires provincial police, who had taken up Francis Galton's work on fingerprint patterns and built from it a workable classification system. By then, La Plata has the first fingerprint file in operation anywhere in the world. In 1904 Vucetich will publish his *Dactiloscopía comparada* (Comparative Fingerprinting), and his classification method will be adopted by many police forces.

Francisca Rojas is convicted. In all likelihood, it is the first criminal conviction in the world obtained through a fingerprint.

## What the trace shifted

What matters about the case is not that a guilty person was found. It is that the innocent man was released without having to convince anyone. Until then, establishing the facts rested on human beings: the confession, the testimony, the reputation, and behind them the coercion that could be used to obtain them. A man with no allies and no social credit had nothing to set against an accusation. The fingerprint brought into the courtroom an element that cannot be intimidated or bought, and that does not depend on the standing of the person it points to.

This is the meaning of the whole movement toward physical evidence over the past century and a half, and the reason the confession slowly lost its status as the queen of proofs. Not because a confession is always false, but because a confession can be manufactured, and the way of manufacturing it was precisely what the neighbor endured while the inspector was looking at the door.

What remained was a belief that would settle in along with the method, and that it would take more than a century to shake: that a fingerprint never errs.

repere.texte: In 1892, the police of La Plata, Argentina, operate the world's first working fingerprint file, built by Juan Vucetich from the work of Francis Galton.

carte.punch: The innocent man didn't have to convince anyone. That is what physical evidence changed.
carte.idee: In 1892 in Necochea, a neighbor is accused of killing two children and questioned relentlessly. An inspector saws out the door panel bearing a bloody print and takes it to La Plata: it is the mother's, Francisca Rojas, who is convicted.
carte.source_courte: NLM, Visible Proofs, Juan Vucetich entry

quiz.question: What does the print found in 1892 provide that the neighbor's interrogation could not?
choix: Evidence faster to obtain than a confession, which allowed him to be freed the same day
Official recognition of his innocence by the provincial authorities
An element that points to its author without depending on what anyone agrees to say
A method already accepted by Argentine courts, unlike testimony
quiz.explication: Confession and testimony pass through people, and therefore through the coercion that can be applied to them, as the treatment inflicted on the neighbor shows. Physical traces establish a fact regardless of what anyone consents to declare.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Inspector Álvarez proceed with the print found on the door?
choix: He saws out the door panel and takes it to La Plata to compare the print
He photographs the print and sends the picture to La Plata by telegraph
He lifts the print with a special powder, then traces it onto paper
He brings Juan Vucetich himself to the scene to examine the door
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rather than describe the print in a report, Álvarez saws out the door panel and takes the piece of wood back to La Plata, where he compares the print with those of the people present.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is Juan Vucetich, under whom Inspector Álvarez trained?
choix: An Italian forensic physician invited by Argentina to modernize its scientific policing
An employee of the Buenos Aires police who turns Galton's work into a classification system
An Argentine judge who presides over Francisca Rojas's trial
A journalist who first broke the story in the Buenos Aires press
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Vucetich is an immigrant from Dalmatia, employed by the Buenos Aires provincial police, who takes up Francis Galton's work on fingerprint patterns to build a workable classification system.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What belief settles in along with the fingerprint method, and takes more than a century to shake?
choix: That the police should never again interrogate a suspect
That only prints lifted from a door can serve as valid evidence
That Juan Vucetich should have patented his method before sharing it with other police forces
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry says so in its last sentence: what remained was a belief that would settle in along with the method, and that it would take more than a century to shake, namely that a fingerprint never errs.
